items.question: In what sense can breath separation count as killing for one already bound by fetters?
premises: Breath separation is here called killing in a specific ritual sense.
The initiation described takes a varied form for one bound by fetters.
By that account the act of killing is not stated as the initiation itself.
items.inference: For one bound by fetters, separation by breath is termed killing, but that killing is not identified with the initiation.
uncertainties: The exact force of dīkṣeyaṃ remains unclear from this verse alone.
It is uncertain whether māraṇaṃ here denotes ritual action or its result.
items.plain_english: For one bound by fetters, separation by breath is indeed called killing, but that killing is not said to be this varied form of initiation.

items.question: On what authority should many animals be given in offering for a god rather than for another purpose?
premises: This arrangement alone applies to an animal offered for a god in an offering.
Reliance falls on a word spoken by a god as the basis for action.
That authority leads to the instruction to give many animals thus.
items.inference: The giving of many animals in offering is not a general rule but an arrangement made for a god on the authority of a god's word.
uncertainties: The scope of yojanā here is uncertain without the surrounding rite context.
It is unclear whether bahūn refers to a fixed number or to an open quantity.
items.plain_english: This is but an arrangement for an animal in offering to a god; relying on a word spoken by a god, one should give many animals thus.

items.question: How does repeated offering across regained bodies lead to the status of a supreme animal after six times?
premises: An offering is made, and a body is obtained again in sequence.
That process is repeated, with offering again, six times in this manner.
The one who undergoes this here becomes a supreme animal of six births.
items.inference: Repeated offering across successive regained bodies, carried out six times, results in the status of a supreme animal marked by six births.
uncertainties: It is unclear whether six births are completed or counted prospectively.
The precise link between regained body and renewed offering remains open.
items.plain_english: Offered once and again obtaining a body, offered again, six times thus: he here becomes a supreme animal of six births.

items.question: By what comparison is it shown that purification does not by itself bestow perfection or liberation?
premises: As gold is purified by order of cooking, so too is the case proclaimed here.
Such purification does not by itself bestow which perfection is in question.
Nor is liberation necessarily attained by that purification alone.
items.inference: Purification is a necessary likeness to refined gold, but like refined gold it does not by itself bestow perfection or bring about liberation.
uncertainties: It is unclear whether the comparison applies to the animal, to the giver, or to both.
The referent of siddhi remains open without wider context.
items.plain_english: As gold is purified by the order of cooking, so too it is proclaimed here: such a one does not by himself bestow any perfection, or is he liberated?

items.question: According to the stated scripture, what consequence follows for one who abandons preparation and acts against vows and goddesses?
premises: It is said in the scripture of bliss that certain actions carry consequence.
One who has mantra preparation but abandons it, reviles vows and goddesses, or gives mantras without basis acts contrary to that teaching.
Such action leads to a stated undesirable consequence.
items.inference: Abandoning mantra preparation and reviling vows or goddesses while giving mantras without basis leads away from the stated goal according to the scripture of bliss.
uncertainties: The exact destination implied by nayāt is not specified in this verse.
The scope of dadyānmantrānvinā remains open to interpretation.
items.plain_english: But it is said in the scripture of bliss: one who, having had mantra preparation, abandons it, reviles vows and goddesses, or gives mantras without them, is led astray.

items.question: What sequence of states is said to follow if one who obtained initiation and mantra abandons them out of delusion?
premises: One obtains initiation, mantra, and related things.
Deluded by son and related things, that one abandons them.
Then attaining a human state, that one again does the same thus.
items.inference: Abandonment out of delusion leads to a human state, and from there the same pattern of action is said to occur again.
uncertainties: It is unclear whether the return to a human state is a fall or a stage in a cycle.
The exact force of api is uncertain from this verse alone.
items.plain_english: Having obtained initiation, mantra, and so on, one deluded by son and so on abandons them; then attaining a human state, one does the same again.

items.question: For what purpose is this twofold being said to be born as two-footed or four-footed for one to seven births?
premises: Thus this being passes through births from one up to seven.
That being is twofold, either two-footed or four-footed.
Such a being is born as an animal for the purpose of an oblation to a goddess.
items.inference: A being who falls into this cycle is born twofold as two-footed or four-footed for one to seven births as an animal for a goddess oblation.
uncertainties: It is unclear whether the count is fixed to seven or extends up to seven.
The relation between the twofold form and the cycle of births remains open.
items.plain_english: Thus this being, twofold as two-footed or four-footed, is born for one to seven births as an animal for the purpose of an oblation to a goddess.

items.question: How can the activity of animals in this offering be considered strange if the offered animal goes to union with Shiva?
premises: This animal, offered by a giver, goes by that door to union with Shiva.
This is to be considered thus.
The activity of those animals is strange in light of that result.
items.inference: Given that an animal offered by a giver goes by that means to union with Shiva, the course of activity for such animals appears strange and calls for consideration.
uncertainties: The referent of taddvārā is not explicit in this verse.
It is unclear what aspect of the animals' activity is meant by citraṃ.
items.plain_english: This animal, offered by a giver, goes by that door to union with Shiva, thus. Considering this, the activity of those animals is strange.

items.question: Why should one not use an animal intended for this offering for enjoyment elsewhere, and remove it if unsuitable?
premises: What is desired for enjoyment should not be done with this animal elsewhere.
This animal is not suitable for that purpose.
Having understood this thus, one should remove that animal.
items.inference: An animal designated for this offering is not to be diverted to enjoyment elsewhere, and if it is not suitable for the offering, one should remove it after understanding that.
uncertainties: The criterion for yogya is not stated in this verse.
It is unclear whether removal means substitution or cessation of offering.
items.plain_english: One should not do what is desired for enjoyment elsewhere with that animal; nor is this animal suitable for it. Having understood this, one should remove it.

items.question: Under what condition may an animal be offered, and how many are to be given according to the stated teaching?
premises: If there is a particular desire, that animal may then be offered.
In that case one should give so many animals, thus.
This is as said by Maheshin.
items.inference: Offering of an animal is not obligatory, but if a particular desire arises, one offers it and gives so many animals as Maheshin has said.
uncertainties: The quantity tāvat is left indefinite in this verse.
The nature of viśeṣa kāṅkṣā is not specified here.
items.plain_english: But if there is a particular desire, one should then offer that animal; one should give so many animals, thus as said by Maheshin.

items.question: Which parts of the animal are to be offered, in what form, and to whom as a supreme offering?
premises: The omentum and marrow of the animal, and these when melted, are taken from the middle of the fire.
They are to be offered to the wheel of Shakti.
This is considered a supreme offering.
items.inference: Melted omentum and marrow of the animal, taken from the middle of the fire, are offered to the wheel of Shakti as a supreme offering.
uncertainties: The procedure for taking from the middle of the fire is not detailed here.
It is unclear whether other parts are excluded by this instruction.
items.plain_english: The omentum and marrow of the animal, and these melted, from the middle of the fire one should offer to the wheel of Shakti; this is considered a supreme offering.

items.question: Which principal parts are to be offered, and is there an alternative set considered more principal?
premises: One should offer the principal parts: heart, intestine, head, shoulder, and liver.
Or one should offer earring, coil, marrow, and axe as what is more principal.
The instruction allows for one of these sets as principal.
items.inference: Two alternative sets of parts are indicated for offering, with the second set presented as more principal in this instruction.
uncertainties: The ritual reason for the alternative set is not stated in this verse.
It is unclear whether karṇikā and kuṇḍalī denote parts or objects here.
items.plain_english: One should offer the principal parts: heart, intestine, head, shoulder, and liver, or alternatively earring, coil, marrow, and axe as what is more principal.
